title: ropeway:handbook-title-50
text: An aerial ropeway carries a cabin across ground you would rather not walk. The haul rope is a loop: one strand runs from tower to tower at sheave height with the cabin's jaw clamped round it, and the other comes back overhead about a block and a third higher. They are the same rope, turned round at each end by a station's bullwheel. The cabin hangs from the lower strand and runs end to end and back again. It carries two people, or two loads of freight, or one of each - a basket or a chest straps onto either bench, which is what these lines were mostly built to do. The words Tower - the gantry you build. A tower with only one span attached is an end tower, and that is where the cabin stops. Station - a tower built on a drive station or tension station footing instead of a plain one. Same sixteen cells, same footprint, same archway: one leg of it is machinery instead of posts. A station replaces a tower in the line, it does not stand beside it. Haul rope - the loop. The going strand is the lower one, at sheave height, that the cabin's jaw is closed on; the return strand is the one overhead, which carries nothing and is what makes the rope a loop rather than a washing line. The gap between them is not a number anyone chose - it is the bullwheel's own diameter, because the wheel is what turns the rope round. Span - one straight stretch of haul rope between two towers. Both strands run every span. Line - all the towers and spans chained end to end. Footing - the pylon footing on the ground. It is the tower: it validates the build, owns the spans and takes every click. Sheave - the split housing in the pylon head that the going strand runs through, four blocks above the footing. Its two cheeks leave a slot down the middle, and the cabin's hanger rides up that slot. Return shoe - the little saddle on the short mast above the sheave, on every pylon head. The return strand rides on it. A station has none: there the wheel is the carrier. Drive housing - the machine that turns the haul rope, at the foot of a drive station's machine leg. An axle runs into any of its four sides, and the shafts above it carry the power up to the bullwheel. It drives the line it is a tower of and no other. A line with no drive station does not move. Tension weight - the mass hanging in a tension station's leg, keeping the haul rope taut. A line will not carry a cabin until one of its towers is a finished tension station. Bullwheel - the big spoked wheel in the middle of a station's crossarm, in place of the pylon head. At the end of a line it is what turns the rope round: the loop arrives on the going strand, wraps half way round the wheel and leaves on the return strand a wheel's diameter higher. It carries no power itself, but its hub axle runs out along the crossarm to the machinery, and it turns whenever the line is running - so you can see from across the valley that the drive is working. On a station the line runs through there is no end to turn, and the wheel stands up on its brackets and presses down on the return strand instead. A plain tower does not take one. Jaw - the clamp at the top of the hanger, closed on the rope itself at sheave height. Station rail - the pair of bars hanging under the crossarm, that the cabin's guide rollers run inside. Each tower draws its own out along the rope in both directions rather than straight across the crossarm, so at a corner the rail curves with the line and opens by exactly as much as the cabin arrives crooked. Building a tower Place a pylon footing on the ground where the tower should stand. It turns to face you, and the whole tower is measured up from it. Look at the placed footing - while the tower is unfinished the block info panel names the two directions the cabin will pass through, so you can turn the footing down the line before building anything. You then place fifteen more blocks by hand: - Two posts of four blocks, standing on the ground three blocks either side of the footing. Wood or dressed stone: logs, debarked logs, planks, raw stone, cobblestone, drystone, polished rock or stone bricks, so the tower can match whatever you build in. Slabs, stairs and soil are not posts. - A seven-wide crossarm across their tops, four blocks up: the pylon head directly above the footing with three ropeway braces either side of it. The two outermost braces are what make the archway five wide rather than three, and that width is what stops the cabin catching a post where the line changes direction. They come nearly free: one brace craft makes eight, and a whole tower wants seven - six on the crossarm and one more inside the pylon head - so that is a single metal plate with one brace over. That is the whole tower - one crossarm, one block deep. It leaves a clear five-wide, four-tall archway, and the cabin threads through it nose first, its hanger up between the sheave cheeks and its jaw closed on the rope. A station is the same sixteen cells and the same archway. Place a drive station footing or a tension station footing instead of the plain one and the overlay asks for machinery down one leg and along half the crossarm rather than posts and braces. Two of a line's towers want to be stations - one of each - and the rest are plain. See Power and the Drive. What it costs Priced in ingots, counting a metal plate as the two ingots it is smithed from and a metal bit as a twentieth of one. Any metal will do; iron is the one to think in. A plain tower - about two ingots, plus eight blocks of whatever you make posts from. One plate becomes all the braces it wants; two metal bits do the rest. Every tower after the first two costs that and no more, which is the whole point: a long line is mostly cheap towers. A span - one haul rope per four blocks, and haul rope comes four to a craft, so you buy a span in whole crafts of two ordinary ropes and a metal bit. A span up to 16 blocks is one craft; 17 to 32 blocks - a 20 or a 30 - is two, four rope and two bits; and the longest span there is, 48 blocks, is three: six rope and three bits. Count crafts rather than blocks; the per-block rate rounds the wrong way on about a third of span lengths. The cabin - half an ingot, four planks and a rope. A drive station - about 16 ingots, three quarters of it the drive head, the housing and the shaft run. A tension station - about 13. Those are once per line, not once per tower, and they are where all the machinery lives. A short line - two stations, one 30-block span and a cabin - comes to roughly 31 ingots: ten metal plates and 215 metal bits, with 15 planks, 11 sticks, 9 loose stones, 9 rope and 8 posts. Three anvils' worth of iron, for the machine and both ends of it together. A 20-block span instead of the 30 saves you one haul-rope craft: 214 bits and 7 rope. A ten-tower mountain route - eight plain towers, two stations and nine 30-block spans - about 46, and 49 rope. It is barely half again as much, because everything past those first two stations is two ingots a tower and four rope a span. Right-click the footing at any time. If the tower is unfinished it tells you how many blocks are missing and lights up every cell that is wrong or empty - red where the wrong block sits, and the colour of the block it wants where nothing is. Every other click a tower takes lands on the footing too; the pylon head up top is only a piece of the frame. Sneak and right-click the footing to open the tower guide: the build order in words, next to a turning 3D view of the six blocks a tower or a station is built from - all three footings, the pylon head, the brace and the bullwheel - and the cabin itself. Next: Building a Line, then Power and the Drive.
